32:1.text: And immediately when Jesus perceived in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, he said unto them, Why reason ye these things in your hearts?

provenance.other: “these things in your hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 2:8. Luke 5:22, the parallel, reads “What reason ye in your hearts?” and Matthew 9:4 reads “Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?” — neither has the demonstrative, and the mediation is therefore decidable on a single word.
provenance.significance: The verse borrows more than the question; it borrows the situation. In Mark, Jesus knows what the scribes are reasoning without being told, and the rhetorical question is the proof that he knows. Nephi opens chapter 32 by claiming exactly that knowledge — “I suppose that ye ponder somewhat in your hearts, concerning that which ye should do” — and then asks the Markan question of his readers. Nine verses later the whole short chapter turns on the same claim, at 32:8: “I perceive that ye ponder still in your hearts.” Mark's “perceived in his spirit” has become Nephi's warrant for addressing objections nobody has voiced, which is the rhetorical engine of the entire chapter.

32:1.note: Nephi's substitution is “ponder” for “reason”, which is Luke's verb elsewhere (Luke 2:19, “Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart”) and softens the rebuke into an invitation. Everything else is Mark's, including the demonstrative that separates Mark from both Synoptic parallels. The frame recurs at 32:8 and is registered there rather than given a second row.

32:4.text: Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.

provenance.route: James 4:2 + Matthew 7:7-8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “because ye ask not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:2 — and the Book of Mormon reproduces the causal conjunction with it: “it will be because ye ask not”. The knocking that follows is Matthew 7:7-8's, the only KJV passage where asking and knocking are paired as conditions of receiving.
provenance.significance: Two sources are fused in six words, and each brings something the other lacks. Matthew 7:7 supplies the pairing of ask and knock; James 4:2 supplies the diagnosis, that the failure is the petitioner's own. The fusion is what makes the sentence work as a rebuke rather than an invitation: Matthew alone would have promised, James alone would have accused, and Nephi needs both because he is explaining why his own writing has not been understood. Recover James 4 and the accusation is sharper still — James's non-askers do not ask because they are at war with each other, and Nephi's chapter is about a people he has just called unbelieving, wicked, ignorant and stiffnecked at 32:7.

32:4.note: “It will be because ye ask not, neither do ye knock; wherefore, ye are not brought into the light, but must perish in the dark.” The James singleton is exact and carries its conjunction; the knocking has no other biblical source than Matthew 7:7-8, where “knock, and it shall be opened unto you” stands with “ask, and it shall be given you” in a single sentence. Note that Nephi has inverted the sequence — Matthew and Luke 11:9 both run ask, seek, knock, and Nephi drops the seeking, which is the middle term and the one his argument has no use for.

32:5.text: Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.

provenance.other: “he will shew you things to come” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 16:13, and “guide you into all truth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. John 14:26's “he shall teach you all things” is the companion promise and stands behind 2 Nephi 31:12; this verse has John 16's verb, not John 14's.
provenance.significance: The two Johannine Paraclete promises are used at two different points and not confused. At 31:12 the Father gives the Holy Ghost and the emphasis is on teaching, which is John 14:26; here the Holy Ghost, once received, will shew, which is John 16:13. Nephi's addition is the object: John's Spirit shews things to come, Nephi's shews “all things what ye should do”. Prophecy has been converted into practical guidance, and that conversion is the answer chapter 32 exists to give — the question at 32:1 was concerning that which ye should do.

32:5.note: The decisive evidence is a spelling the modern text no longer has. 1830 reads “it will shew unto you all things”; the 1920 edition changed “shew” to “show”, and with it went the only surface trace of John 16:13's verb, which the KJV also spells “shew”. This is the case CONVENTIONS §8 describes exactly: the first edition displays a borrowing that the current text conceals. Confidence is high rather than certain because the shared run is short and the collocation of Spirit with shewing is not unique to John; what carries it is that this chapter has already used John 14:26 one chapter earlier and is plainly working through the Farewell Discourse.

32:6.text: All the commandments which I command thee this day shall ye observe to do, that ye may live, and multiply, and go in and possess the land which the LORD sware unto your fathers.

provenance.other: “shall ye observe to do” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 8:1. The bare “observe to do” is a Deuteronomic formula and appears a dozen times (5:32, 6:3, 12:32, 24:8 among them), but always with a different subject placement; the inverted clause with the postposed subject pronoun is Deuteronomy 8:1's alone.
provenance.significance: The frame matters more than the words. Deuteronomy 8:1 makes what Moses commands this day the thing to be observed; 2 Nephi 32:6 makes what Christ shall say when he manifests himself in the flesh the thing to be observed, and says in the same breath that “there will be no more doctrine given” until then. A Deuteronomic sentence about the sufficiency of the law delivered at Horeb has been rewritten as a statement about a doctrine that is closed until a future appearance. If the echo is real, the canon-closing move is being made in the words of the canon-closing chapter of the Pentateuch's own farewell discourse.

32:6.note: Five words in the same inverted order, from a single KJV verse. Kept at moderate and typed as an echo because “observe to do” is genuinely formulaic in Deuteronomy and a nineteenth-century writer steeped in the KJV could produce the inversion without Deuteronomy 8 in view. It earns its row because the sentence it stands in is the chapter's doctrinal hinge and because the frame — a body of commandment declared complete — is Deuteronomy's, not just its phrasing.
32:6.whyNot: A Deuteronomic idiom used dozens of times in the book it comes from, and the identification of Deuteronomy 8:1 in particular rests on word order rather than on distinctive vocabulary. Nothing else in 2 Nephi 32 touches Deuteronomy.

32:8.text: Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.

provenance.other: “the Spirit itself maketh intercession” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:26. It is the Bible's only statement that the Spirit's office is to supply what human prayer lacks, which is the proposition 2 Nephi 32:8 needs.
provenance.significance: Nephi's claim is that the disposition to pray is itself diagnostic — the Spirit teaches a man to pray, the evil spirit teaches him that he must not. That claim has one biblical foundation and this is it: Romans 8:26 is the only place where the Spirit is said to be involved in the act of praying rather than in its answer. Note also what Nephi does not take. Paul's Spirit intercedes with groanings which cannot be uttered, and Nephi has just said at 32:7 that “the spirit stoppeth mine utterance”. The unutterable is on both sides of the borrowing, but Paul's is the Spirit's speech and Nephi's is his own silence.

32:8.note: No KJV run is reproduced, so this is conceptual and moderate: the argument is that the doctrine has a single biblical home and that Nephi is standing in it. Romans 8:26 supplies the Spirit as the agent of prayer; 2 Nephi 32:8 turns that agency into a test of spirits, which is a step Paul does not take and which owes something to 1 John 4:1-3. `kjvSpecific` is 'uncertain' by design — there is no phrasing here to test against any English version.
32:8.whyNot: A conceptual link with no verbal contact at all beyond the pairing of spirit and prayer, which is common ground in any Christian devotional writing of the period. A reader who declines it loses nothing from the chapter's other links.

32:9.text: And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;

provenance.other: “always to pray” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 18:1, and “pray, and not to faint” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The pairing of continual prayer with fainting is unique to it: 1 Thessalonians 5:17's “Pray without ceasing” has the continuity and not the fainting, and Galatians 6:9's “let us not be weary in well doing” has neither.
provenance.significance: Nephi's one change is grammatical and it changes the force entirely. Luke's sentence is descriptive and third-person — Jesus spoke a parable to the end that MEN OUGHT always to pray. Nephi's is imperative and second-person: “ye must pray always, and not faint.” An observation about what is fitting has become a commandment, and the modal has moved from ought to must, which is the same move the chapter makes at 32:6 with Deuteronomy's “shall ye observe to do” and at 33:15 with “I must obey”. The verse then adds the manner from John 16:23 — pray to the Father in the name of Christ — so that the last instruction in Nephi's writing is Luke's persistence performed by John's route.

32:9.note: Seven of nine words in sequence, from the single KJV verse that holds them, with the word order of “always to pray” reversed to “pray always” — a reversal the Book of Mormon makes consistently and which does not weaken the identification, since the two rare collocations of the verse are both present. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his 36. The remainder of the verse takes “ye shall pray unto the Father in the name of Christ” from John 16:23, where “ask the Father in my name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the substitution of praying for asking is Nephi's, and it is the substitution the whole chapter has been arguing for since 32:4.
